reason: The sources thoroughly corroborate over twenty detailed technical and historical claims across multiple independent sites regarding the first photograph from the surface of Venus.
story: In October 1975, the Soviet Union dropped a 660-kilogram armored titanium sphere through the blistering skies of Venus. Scientists anticipated a pitch-black, sandblasted wasteland crushed under ninety atmospheres of pressure. Instead, Venera 9 pulled off the impossible: it touched down upright on a twenty-degree volcanic slope in Beta Regio and became the first spacecraft to photograph the surface of another world. When its mechanical scanner relayed the line-by-line image to the orbiter overhead, scientists were stunned. Venus wasn't dark at all. Sunlight filtered through the dense clouds like an overcast afternoon on Earth, illuminating flat, sharp-edged volcanic rocks that had never been worn smooth by water or wind. Even though one camera lens cap failed to pop off and searing heat hovered around 460 degrees Celsius, Venera 9 transmitted for fifty-three remarkable minutes before the relay orbiter slipped below the horizon, forever changing our picture of Earth's twisted twin.
angle: The first photograph ever taken from another planet's surface revealed daylight bright enough to read by and sharp, uneroded rocks on Venus, shattering decades of predictions of a pitch-black, sandblasted plain.

claims.claim: Venera 9 was launched on June 8, 1975.
Venera 9 was launched using a Proton booster rocket.
The Venera 9 mission comprised an orbiter and a detachable lander.
The Venera 9 orbiter became the first spacecraft to enter orbit around Venus.
The lander separated from the orbiter on October 20, 1975.
The lander made touchdown on Venus at 05:13 UTC on October 22, 1975.
Venera 9 returned the first image ever taken on the surface of another planet.
The lander touched down in the upland volcanic region of Beta Regio.
The lander came to rest on an incline of approximately 20 degrees.
The surface payload mass of the lander was 660 kilograms.
The lander entered the Venusian atmosphere at an initial velocity of 10.7 kilometers per second.
The parachute was released at an altitude of 50 kilometers, allowing aerodynamic braking through the thick lower atmosphere.
The aerodynamic shield slowed the lander to a final descent speed of roughly 7 meters per second at touchdown.
The lander operated and transmitted surface telemetry for 53 minutes.
Lander transmissions ended because the relay orbiter moved out of radio range below the horizon.
A protective lens cover on one of the two cameras failed to separate, preventing a full 360-degree panoramic image.
The photograph revealed flat, sharp-edged rocks and slabs rather than an eroded, sand-covered plain.
Natural daylight illumination on the surface was comparable to an overcast day on Earth.
The orbiter was used as a real-time communications relay to transmit lander data back to Earth.
Atmospheric pressure on the surface of Venus was measured at approximately 90 atmospheres or bar.
Thermal management utilized interior pre-cooling prior to atmospheric entry and circulating fluid loops.

disputed: Surface temperature: S1 reports 485 degrees Celsius, S5 reports 455 degrees Celsius, S6 cites 465 to 470 degrees Celsius, and S7 reports 480 degrees Celsius; a script should state 'over 450 degrees Celsius' or attribute specific figures.

Cause of signal loss: Popular legacy accounts claimed the lander was instantly crushed or fried after 53 minutes, but mission data confirms contact was lost because the relay orbiter drifted beyond the horizon; a script should state that transmission ceased when the orbiter dropped out of view.

Atmospheric entry speed unit: S3 mistakenly lists the speed as 10.7 kilometers per hour, whereas S1 and S5 correctly identify it as 10.7 kilometers per second; a script should use kilometers per second.
Exact panorama field of view: S1 and S3 describe the resulting image as 180 degrees, while S5 specifies 174 degrees; a script should describe it as 'roughly 180 degrees'.

sources.title: In October 1975, the Soviet Venera 9 probe survived just 53 minutes on the surface of Venus before the 465°C heat and 92-atmosphere pressure crushed it, but in those 53 minutes it sent back the first photograph ever taken from the surface of another planet — grainy, black-and-white, and showing sharp-edged rocks nobody had expected to still be intact.
